Created and led by Peasant Smith (@mw00), co-maintained with @needmorevram


Project Maya is free. If it runs well on your PC, a coffee keeps the work on it going.

Models this size usually need a datacenter. Maya runs **[GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash)** (zai-org, MIT license; 321 B parameters, about 18 B active per token, a context of up to 1 M tokens) and **[DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017)** (DeepSeek, MIT license; 748 B parameters) on the hardware you already have. Each model has an engine built for it. It keeps the experts your conversation uses most on the GPU, the next ones in RAM and the rest on your NVMe SSD, and moves them as you chat. It measures your GPUs, CPU, RAM and SSD and tunes itself to them. Nothing leaves your machine. - **Fast:** up to 124 tokens/s on two H100s, 118 on four RTX 4090s, 81 on one RTX PRO 6000, 30+ on a single RTX 5090. Real numbers from real users below. - **Close to the original:** Maya's own quants of GLM-5.3-Flash keep 97.7-99.2% of the FP8 model's zero-shot accuracy; DeepSeek V4.1 · Maya-S picks the same next token as the original 92.6% of the time. - **Plugs into your tools:** OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API with tool calls, ready for coding agents. - **Several requests at once:** up to 8 answered together - for agents that run several sessions, or several people on one PC. - **Everything in the box:** a chat and a live monitor in the browser, pictures, thinking levels, a one-command setup. ## The models Every Maya quant is named after its model first, then its tier - XS, S, M or L, by how many bits its experts keep - so "GLM-5.3 · Maya-S" and "MiniMax M3.1 · Maya-S" never get mixed up. The setup asks which one to download; to pick one yourself, give its setup id: `./setup.sh --model glm-maya-s24`. The names used before (`--model Maya-S24`, `--ds4-quant maya-xs`, ...) keep working. Project Maya's own quants of GLM-5.3-Flash, made from Z.ai's FP8 release with statistics from the FP8 model. Other shapes, other quant types, other architectures and CUDA keep the original dispatch. Set `MAYA_HIP_EXPERTS_LEGACY=1` before starting a process to force original HIP expert kernels for an end-to-end comparison. The main change is packed sign expansion: a multiply spreads four sign bits into the high bit of four bytes, then masks and shifts produce the XOR masks and two's-complement corrections. Codebook bytes are positive and nonzero, so ordinary word addition introduces no carries between bytes. This replaces HIP's emulated packed compare/subtract while retaining the original integer scale divisions, FP32 accumulation order, clamping, q8_1 quantization and expert combine order. Gate/up retains sixteen wave32 waves per workgroup, two gate and two up rows per wave, its 2 KiB codebook in LDS, and the fused shared-down branch. Down uses two output rows per workgroup instead of four on optimized paths, reducing its register budget. IQ2_S reads its 8 KiB codebook through global memory; IQ3_XXS keeps its 1 KiB codebook in LDS. The grid selection and sign operations are HIP-only. The signed-codebook technique was adapted from [Strata's moe_fused_iq.cu](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/blob/fb58e0dbc8399662c0e47c76578c6e878b14f6cf/src/prefill/moe_fused_iq.cu) (MIT). Its HIP sign lookup tables were measured first; direct sign arithmetic performed better here. The benchmark retains alternatives for reproducible comparison: sign LUTs, global/LDS codebooks, eight/sixteen gate waves, two/four/eight down rows, alignment-safe eight-byte IQ2_XXS/IQ3_XXS quant loads, a separate shared-down launch, and an eight-wave occupancy constraint. Wider loads, splitting shared down, and the occupancy constraint did not beat the selected paths. This work does not fuse gate/up and down into one kernel. ## Reproduce ```bash cmake -S . -B build-multi -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \ -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/rocm-7.2.1 \ -DCMAKE_HIP_COMPILER=/opt/rocm-7.2.1/llvm/bin/clang++ \ -DMAYA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DMAYA_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF \ -DMAYA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON -DMAYA_NATIVE_EXPERTS=ON \ -DMAYA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF \ -DMAYA_GGML_DIR=/ai/github/project-maya/third_party/llama.cpp \ '-DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1100;gfx1201;gfx1151' CCACHE_DIR=/tmp/maya-experts-ccache cmake --build build-multi -j 8 \ --target maya hip_expert_kernel_bench glm_ffn_parity glm_layer_parity \ glm_model_test iq1_s_parity hip_intrinsics export HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/rocm/lib build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench --shared build-multi/hip_expert_kernel_bench --parity-only --sweep build-multi/glm_ffn_parity --selftest build-multi/glm_layer_parity --selftest build-multi/glm_model_test --selftest build-multi/iq1_s_parity build-multi/hip_intrinsics ``` Run these commands from the repository root. `--sweep` also works with timing; without it the benchmark compares original kernels against production dispatch. Setup puts the card with more VRAM first (it takes the bigger first half), leaves the split point to the engine, and writes one hipBLASLt table per architecture (`MAYA_HIPBLASLT_TUNING` takes a `:`-separated list; each card uses the table for its own architecture). A discrete GPU paired with a unified-memory APU puts the discrete GPU first and loads the parts sequentially (`MAYA_GLM_PARALLEL_LOAD=0`), so the APU sizes its pool after the first part pins its RAM tier. The two cards may be different architectures. The split passes one small host-memory hop per token, so no peer-to-peer access between the cards is needed. Where those bytes come from decides everything: * VRAM cache (hot experts, profile-ranked): unchanged machinery, same hit-rate economics, but each hit now removes 3.2× more bytes from the RAM/SSD path. * RAM (page cache or pinned): on 128 GB machines, ~86 GB of Q2_0-class experts fit alongside the OS - the mmap source with a warm page cache is then DRAM-speed and the current low-RAM mode *is* the main mode. On 64 GB machines roughly half the expert set fits; the rest pages from SSD, and a cache-miss heavy token costs ~1.2 GB of NVMe reads ≈ 100-150 ms - workable at ~5-8 tok/s cold, degraded but usable, and the expert profile is what keeps the miss rate down over time. * SSD: NVMe random reads at blob granularity (~7 MB) are exactly the access pattern the existing mmap source and the PLE reader's unbuffered async path (`direct_file.hpp`) were built for. What the engine already has for this: `FileExpertSource` (MapViewOfFile/mmap, blob = base + multiply, `expert_source.hpp:303-360`), `pin_cache_complement` (pin the non-cached complement when RAM allows), the VRAM tier with decayed-usage swapping, PCIe streaming of next-layer experts during prefill attention, KV streaming, and the unbuffered async file layer. One lesson the code already holds, and the study adopts: **retention is the whole game, and random-access hints are the enemy.** `FILE_FLAG_RANDOM_ACCESS` was tried on the expert mapping and measured at **1.93 GB/s - disk speed, 14x off** - because it tells Windows' cache manager to drop the pages again quickly (`expert_source.cpp:332-343`). The expert access pattern is random per layer but *repeated every token*, so the mapping deliberately carries no hint at all. The same reasoning rules out `MADV_RANDOM` on Linux. What a 100 GB+ mapping does need (implemented on this branch, §7): 1. **Prefetch the routed blobs at `begin_layer`.** The source's own contract says it: "a source that reads from disk wants to start the read here so it overlaps the quantisation" (`expert_source.hpp:98`). When the router's ids for a layer are known, issuing `PrefetchVirtualMemory` (Windows) / `posix_fadvise(WILLNEED)` (Linux) for exactly those k blobs page-ins them while the pool quantizes the activation and the GPU finishes the previous layer - the mmap-path analogue of the PCIe expert streaming the prefill path already does. Unlike the random-access flag, prefetch is *retention-friendly*: it pulls the pages the router will actually touch into the standby list and says nothing about evicting the rest. 2. **Keep the mapping hint-free.** At GLM's scale (~86-162 GB of experts) the temptation to "fix" random access with hints is stronger and the failure mode is the same measured one. The mapping stays undecorated; the page cache decides retention by recency, which is what a hot working set inside a much larger mapped file wants. 3. **Never map-and-pin by accident.** `pin_cache_complement` remains opt-in and is now also the tool for the 128 GB-RAM case (pin the complement the VRAM cache does not hold, when it fits); on 64 GB it must stay off and the page cache must be allowed to reclaim. ## 5. Expected performance envelope (estimates, ±30 %) The method: GPU part scaled by bandwidth and VRAM-held expert share, CPU part by remaining expert bytes. Assume an RTX 3090-class card (24 GB) + DDR5, Q2_0-class pack: * ~3,000 VRAM-cached experts cover ~70 % of reads (profile economics transfer; per-expert bytes are 3.2× bigger, so a 24 GB card caches ~2.5-3 K of them). This works for scalar K-quants and for the IQ lattice types, since a block is a block. - **Candidates**: - routed experts: IQ1_M, IQ2_XXS, IQ2_XS, IQ2_S, IQ3_XXS, IQ3_S, IQ4_XS - everything else: Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K, Q8_0 - **Recorded**: the Hessian-weighted output error per (tensor, type) and per expert group. - **Cost control**: the error table needs a sample of experts per layer (~32 of 288). Only the final assembly quantizes everything. - **Gumbel-softmax refinement**: the paper's Gumbel-softmax training of the grid choices and scales, published for scalar K-quants. It's a later add-on for any K-quant tensors the allocation picks, kept only if it measurably lowers KL. ### 4. Allocation (RCO-style) - **Goal**: choose a type per tensor under the byte budget, minimizing predicted end-to-end damage (each tensor's error times its layer's sensitivity, with sensitivity from small perturbation runs). Then score the top 2-3 allocations in our engine against the FP8 reference and keep the best. RCO proper uses gradients of the true KL; this approximates it with measured errors plus measured KL checks. - **Maya-specific: per-expert bits.** Our engine loads its own pack, so experts don't all need the same type. - Hot experts (high routing frequency and saliency) get more bits; the long tail gets fewer. - The GGUF version keeps one type per tensor so it still loads in llama.cpp. - Usage on real text is very skewed (that is why Mercury's VRAM tier hits 97%), so this should buy more quality per GB than anything else. - **Fixed floors against loops and drift**. These parts are only ~6 GB: - attention, MLA, KDA and shared experts at Q6_K-Q8_0 - the 3 dense layers at Q8_0 - output head Q6_K or better, embeddings Q6_K - down never below gate/up for the same expert ### 5. Pruning study (Maya-S only) Pruning frees bytes, but it is not free: - OpenMOSE's REAP prune of this exact model (60 of 288 experts per layer removed) measured KL 0.45 against the original, and perplexity +2.8%. - The public 3.5 -> 3.0-bit step costs about 0.07 KL. So: budget-matched runs at 0%, ~10% and ~20% pruning, each with the bits the freed bytes buy, judged by KL, task checks and the loop test. My expectation is that light or no pruning wins and per-expert bits do the work. ### 6. Assembly - **GGUF**: standard types, one type per tensor, loads in llama.cpp. Metadata comes from today's GGUF. - **Maya pack**: what our engine loads, including per-expert types when used. - **Vision**: the mmproj stays BF16 (1.2 GB) for the day the engine gets vision. ### 7. Evaluation (each candidate, the same text) - **KL against the FP8 reference**, plus perplexity and top-1 agreement: - on the held-out mix - separately for chat, code, math and Portuguese - long context (16-32k) - **Loop test**: 50 long generations at the default sampling (T=1.0, top-p 0.95) and 20 greedy ones. Measures repeated n-grams, runs that never end, and broken thinking-block structure. - **Task accuracy against the FP8 model** (zero-shot ARC-Easy/Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA the way lm-evaluation-harness scores them: tools/maya_quant/zs_*.py), and spot checks: - GSM8K (100) - HumanEval subset - IFEval subset - MMLU-Pro (300) - a Portuguese chat set - **Speed** on Uranus (64 + 32) and Mercury. ## Engine work (Mercury/Uranus) - **Done 2026-10-06: the decode kernels** for IQ2_XS 17, IQ2_S 22, IQ3_S 21 and IQ1_M 29, beside IQ2_XXS 16, IQ3_XXS 18, IQ1_S 19, IQ4_XS 23, Q2_K 10 and Q3_K 11. - Checked on synthetic experts against a double-precision reference: every type lands at the same ~1.5% (expert kernels) and ~0.9% (dense GEMV), which is the q8_1 activation's share. - The prompt path's MMQ now also builds Q2_K-Q6_K. - The CPU lane goes through ggml, which covers every type. - **IQ1_M has no MMQ in llama.cpp**, so a layer of it couldn't go through the batched prompt path. Not started; the owner decides when. # Responses API Maya accepts `POST /v1/responses`, with JSON or SSE output, using the same model, authentication, CORS policy, context limit, and generation engine as Chat Completions. This includes GLM models served by `maya` and DeepSeek-V4.1 models served by `maya-ds4`, with their configured chat templates, tool syntax and vision paths. ```sh curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/responses \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"input":"Hello","store":false,"stream":true,"max_output_tokens":256}' ``` With the OpenAI Python SDK: ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1", api_key="your-key-or-any-text") response = client.responses.create( model="your-model", input="Hello", store=False, ) print(response.output_text) ``` ## Supported behavior - String `input`, or a full history containing user, assistant, system and developer messages. `instructions` supplies system instructions for this request. - `input_text`, `output_text` in history, and `input_image` with an `image_url` (including data URLs). Images use the configured vision encoder; only the `auto` detail mode is supported. Function results may contain text and image parts. - Function tools with `name`, `description`, `parameters`, and optional `strict`. `tool_choice` accepts `auto`, `none`, `required`, or `{"type":"function","name":"..."}`. Calls to undeclared or disallowed functions fail the response. Required/named choices must produce a complete call. `parallel_tool_calls:false` stops generation at the first complete call, with the tokens actually consumed reported in usage. - Truncated function calls have `status:"incomplete"` and do not emit a completed function-arguments event. An end-of-turn inside an unfinished call fails the response. `strict:true` enables schema validation before any generated content or executable arguments are published; omitted/false strict does not enforce schemas. - `function_call` output and `function_call_output` history, matched by `call_id`. A group of function results can arrive in a different order from its calls. All calls need their results in the input before generation can continue. - `reasoning.effort`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_output_tokens`, and `metadata`. Reasoning is returned as a `reasoning` item with `reasoning_text` content, and can be replayed in history. It is plain model reasoning, not a generated summary. - SSE response/item/content lifecycles, text and function-argument deltas, and final usage. Hitting the output limit yields `response.incomplete` with `incomplete_details.reason="max_output_tokens"`; an engine failure yields `response.failed`. Disconnecting stops foreground generation; background generation continues independently of a reader. - `prompt_cache_key` is a validated optional cache hint (up to 256 characters), echoed in the response. Native prompt-prefix reuse determines actual cache hits; the hint does not partition or force the engine cache. String-valued `client_metadata` is accepted as diagnostic context and is not stored or echoed. - The `include:["reasoning.encrypted_content"]` projection is accepted only with explicit `reasoning.effort:"none"`, when there are no reasoning items to encrypt. Encryption and encrypted reasoning input remain unsupported. ## Conversation State Responses are **not stored by default**, including when `store` is omitted. With `store:false`, send the full history. For example, append `response.output` and the matching tool results to the original input before requesting the next turn: ```python history = [{"role": "user", "content": "Look up alpha"}] response = client.responses.create(model="your-model", input=history, tools=tools, store=False) history += [item.to_dict() for item in response.output] for item in response.output: if item.type == "function_call": result = execute_function(item.name, item.arguments) history.append({"type": "function_call_output", "call_id": item.call_id, "output": result}) response = client.responses.create(model="your-model", input=history, tools=tools, store=False) ``` For server-managed history, opt in with `store:true` and use `previous_response_id` on the next request. Only the new messages or function results need to be sent: ```python first = client.responses.create(model="your-model", input="Remember the value 73", store=True) second = client.responses.create( model="your-model", previous_response_id=first.id, input="What value did I give you?", store=True, ) saved = client.responses.retrieve(second.id) items = list(client.responses.input_items.list(second.id, order="asc", limit=20)) client.responses.delete(first.id) ``` A response containing a function call can be continued with just its matching `function_call_output` items and `previous_response_id`. Declare the available tools again in each request. **Instructions and generation settings are not inherited**: `instructions` applies only to the current request. An earlier explicit system or developer message in `input` remains part of conversation history. `store:false` can also continue a stored response, but its new result is not saved. Successful and output-limited responses are saved before their terminal event is sent. Failed or disconnected foreground generations are not stored. A stored response becomes available only when generation finishes. Background tasks have a separately bounded live record and event history as described below. ### Retention and Isolation - Storage is **in memory**, per running Maya service; it does not survive a restart. - At most **128 cached responses** and **64 MiB of serialized unique item blocks, response metadata and item references** are kept by default. Python object overhead, request-owned expanded histories and background records are separate. - Responses expire **one hour after completion**, even if read again. Access and insertion discard expired entries; capacity pressure evicts least recently used entries. A single oversized snapshot fails with a storage-capacity error. - Records are isolated by the authenticated API key. Bearer and `x-api-key` forms of the same key share access. Without configured authentication, all callers share the same cache, just as they share access to the model. - Expired, evicted, deleted, unknown and other-key IDs return HTTP 404, including when supplied as `previous_response_id`. History is never silently dropped. - Snapshots reference shared immutable JSON items within one credential scope. Deleting an ancestor does not delete its items while a descendant still references them. Input IDs and pagination order stay stable, without recursive parent lookups. - Concurrent snapshot assembly has its own serialized-byte admission limit; pressure returns HTTP 503 rather than dropping history. Limits and optional owner quotas are documented in [Responses settings](#settings-and-metrics). ### Resource Endpoints | Method | Path | Behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | GET | `/v1/responses/{id}` | Retrieve the saved final response | | DELETE | `/v1/responses/{id}` | Delete that snapshot | | GET | `/v1/responses/{id}/input_items` | List its full input history, excluding its own output | | POST | `/v1/responses/{id}/cancel` | Request cancellation of a background task | Input lists accept `order=asc|desc` (default `desc`), `limit=1..100` (default 20), and `after=`. Item IDs stay stable across pages. The OpenAI SDK's automatic pagination is supported. Background retrieval also accepts `stream=true` and an optional nonnegative `starting_after` sequence number. Deletion accepts no query options; additional `include` fields remain unsupported. ## Structured Output `text.format` accepts `text`, `json_object`, or `json_schema`. Schema output uses `name`, `schema`, and optional boolean `strict`: ```python response = client.responses.create( model="your-model", input="Return the count", text={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "name": "count", "strict": True, "schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"count": {"type": "integer"}}, "required": ["count"], "additionalProperties": False}}}, ) ``` Schemas use Draft 2020-12 validation from `jsonschema`. The supported subset includes objects/properties/required/additionalProperties, arrays/items, enum/const/anyOf, basic and nullable types, numeric bounds/multipleOf, string length and array length. The root must be an object. Strict object schemas must set `additionalProperties:false` and require every property; optional values can be represented with a nullable type. References, definitions, patterns, formats, conditionals and unknown keywords are rejected before generation. Limits: 64 KiB, 512 schema nodes and 24 schema nesting levels. This is **validate-before-publish**, not token-level constrained decoding. JSON instructions are added to the model prompt. When structured output or a strict tool is requested, generated events are buffered (4 MiB estimated byte/object budget). Only a fully valid completed result is published. Invalid JSON, wrong types or schema violations produce `response.failed` with consumed usage, without publishing invalid text/tool deltas. No automatic generation retries are performed. An output limit yields `response.incomplete` with usage and no unvalidated content. This changes streaming latency: lifecycle/keep-alive events arrive first, content and argument events arrive after validation. Validation accepts at most 65,536 instance nodes and 32 instance nesting levels, with a one-second budget checked during schema traversal and cancellation checks. JSON parsing itself is bounded by the buffer size. Ordinary text does not require the `jsonschema` import; standard setup installs it for structured/schema output. Use `client.responses.parse(..., text_format=YourPydanticModel)` for supported Pydantic schemas; models generating unsupported keywords are rejected explicitly. ## Background Tasks and Recovery `background:true` requires explicit `store:true`: ```python job = client.responses.create(model="your-model", input="Long request", background=True, store=True) current = client.responses.retrieve(job.id) for event in client.responses.retrieve(job.id, stream=True): pass # Reconnect strictly after a previously received sequence number: for event in client.responses.retrieve(job.id, stream=True, starting_after=last_sequence): pass cancelled = client.responses.cancel(job.id) ``` Creation returns a queued response; background+stream can attach immediately. Workers own preparation, image embeddings, generation and cleanup. The existing engine FIFO still controls actual GPU access. A disconnected reader does not stop the task. Ordinary foreground disconnects continue to stop generation. Queries expose queued/in_progress and a single completed/incomplete/failed/cancelled terminal state. Cancellation removes queued jobs without starting generation; running cancellation signals the generator, waits for cleanup, and only then publishes cancelled. The cancel call waits up to five seconds; a slow backend may still return in_progress and must be polled. A running image encoder operation must return/clean up before cancellation completes. No cancelled state is fabricated while the worker still owns resources. Deadline expiry fails the task after cleanup. Cancellation is idempotent. Its SSE stream terminates with the standard `error` event (`code:"response_cancelled"`); the authoritative response snapshot has `status:"cancelled"`. No nonstandard `response.cancelled` event is emitted. Active tasks cannot be deleted (409); cancel them first. Cancelled/failed responses cannot be used as previous_response_id. Running tasks cannot yet be continued (409). Background records are independent of cache LRU: by default at most 16 records, two workers, four active tasks per key, 300-second admission-to-finish deadline, 2 MiB input snapshots per task and 900 seconds of completed-record retention. Completed records can be evicted early to admit new tasks; active ones cannot. Their snapshots remain retrievable and can supply continuation history during retention even if the ordinary response cache evicts its copy. This is additional bounded storage, separate from the ordinary cache's TTL/byte limit. Event buffers retain at most 4096 events / 2 MiB per task. A slow reader whose cursor falls behind gets HTTP 410 before streaming, or a terminal standard SSE `error` event if already connected. Future cursors get 400; a known response whose event record is no longer retained gets 409 for streaming retrieval. Full snapshot retrieval remains available while either record/cache retains it. No events are silently skipped. Oversized events fail the task explicitly. Reader admission is bounded globally/per key and slow socket writes time out; reader disconnects free their slot without cancelling background generation. Queue/owner admission pressure returns 429; an oversized input snapshot returns 413. All resource, event and cancellation operations use the same credential isolation. Shutdown stops admission, cancels queued/running jobs and joins workers. A backend that has not released resources within the shutdown wait raises an explicit cleanup error rather than claiming successful cancellation. ## Settings and Metrics All values are integer server settings, read at Service creation. Put them in the config's `env` block, or export them before starting Maya.
